description:
Solobeat is a one-person team from Yangon. I build practical web tools on NASA open data.

For Space Apps 2026 I'm working on Mee ("fire" in Burmese) for the MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge. Mee merges NASA's MODIS and VIIRS fire detections into one consistent record, shows when and where each township burns, compares this season with normal, and sends alerts when fire activity rises. I'm starting with Myanmar, where the dry-season haze comes back every year.
summary:
Mee is a free fire calendar for every township in Myanmar, built on NASA FIRMS active fire data. Five satellites have recorded Myanmar's fire activity since 2000, but each sees fire differently: in 2019, NOAA-20 recorded 313,048 fire detections over Myanmar and MODIS recorded 56,667. On one chart, the record jumps whenever a satellite starts or stops, so nobody can tell whether a fire season is really unusual.

Mee fixes this. On days when two satellites watched together, it measures how differently they count for each state and month, and adjusts every satellite to the NOAA-20 reference scale. We tested this on 2024, a year left out of the fitting: the error in Myanmar's yearly total fell from 82% too low to 3% too high.

The result is one comparable record from 2001 to today. For any township, people see every past fire season, whether this week and this month are normal or higher than usual, and can download the data for any dates. Mee updates itself every morning and sends Telegram alerts in Burmese and English.
details:
What it does

Mee answers one question for fire, forest and disaster teams in Myanmar: is this week normal for my township?

Each of Myanmar's 330 townships, its 14 states and regions, and the whole country has a page with a calendar of daily fire detections from 2001 to yesterday, a chart comparing every fire season, this month so far against the usual for this month, a plain summary of when the season usually starts and peaks, and a year-by-year table.

People find their township by name, by latitude and longitude, or with "Use my location", and can download daily counts as a CSV for any date range. Anyone can follow a township on Telegram (@mee_fire_bot) and get a message at 08:00 when its fire activity level changes. People can also share their location with the bot and choose 10, 25 or 50 km; Mee checks every hour and sends a message when a new fire is detected within that distance. The website and the bot work in Burmese and English.

How it works

1. Collect: NASA FIRMS active-fire detections over Myanmar, from MODIS on Terra (2000 onward) and Aqua (2002 onward), and VIIRS on Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 (2012 onward). About 15.5 million cleaned detections in and around Myanmar; each detection inside Myanmar is assigned to its township.

2. Line up: On days when two satellites both observed, Mee compares their detection counts for each state and month and calculates a scaling factor relative to NOAA-20. Where a state and month have too few detections, it uses the national value for that month. Before July 2002, only Terra was operating, so those days are first adjusted using the typical combined Terra and Aqua counts.

3. Compare: Each township's last 7 days are compared with the same period in previous years, giving normal, higher than usual, or much higher than usual.

4. Update: A scheduled job downloads the newest NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 detections every morning at 06:10 Myanmar time, recalculates the data and publishes the results. Township alerts are sent at 08:00, and nearby fire alerts are checked every hour.

Does it work?

We left 2024 out of the calibration fitting, then rebuilt 2024 from MODIS data alone and compared the results against NOAA-20 observations.

For Myanmar's annual total, the error improved from 82% too low to 3% too high. Across 578 state-week comparisons, typical weekly error improved from 81% to 31%, while weekly correlation increased from 0.97 to 0.98.

The quick morning update matches a full rebuild within 2%.

These results show much better agreement with NOAA-20, especially for annual totals, while also showing that uncertainty remains at shorter time scales.

Why scale counts instead of matching single fires?

A fire calendar needs comparable detection counts per day and place, not a decision about whether one MODIS pixel and one VIIRS pixel represent the same fire.

The satellites pass at different times and detect different sizes of fire, so pixel matching can miss or double-count detections. Scaling counts to the NOAA-20 reference keeps the historical observations and allows validation against a year excluded from fitting.

We chose NOAA-20 as the reference because it provides an ongoing VIIRS record that can connect older satellite data with current observations.

Why it matters

Terra and Aqua are near the end of their missions, and older satellites will keep being replaced by newer ones. Without harmonization, changes in which satellites are flying can create artificial jumps or drops in Myanmar's 25-year fire record.

With Mee, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 can carry the comparable record forward, and future satellites can be added using the same calibration approach.

Fires and smoke affect Myanmar every dry season. Fire, forest and disaster teams need to know early whether current activity is unusual compared with previous years.

How it is creative

NASA FIRMS, Global Forest Watch and GWIS provide valuable fire-monitoring data, but their tools have different priorities and levels of localization.

Mee brings together five satellites into one comparable historical record, organizes the results by Myanmar's own townships, provides a Burmese-language interface, and sends Telegram alerts when activity becomes unusual or a new fire is detected nearby.

It is designed to work well on phones and on slower internet connections.

Who it helps

Disaster and forest teams planning for the fire season, farmers and village leaders, health workers dealing with smoke, and researchers and reporters who need a comparable long-term fire activity record.

Tools

Python and DuckDB for data processing; Next.js, React and Tailwind CSS for the website; GitHub Actions for daily updates; Vercel for hosting; and Upstash Redis and the Telegram Bot API for alerts. Claude (Anthropic) was used as an AI coding assistant during development.

The project source code is publicly available under the MIT license.
